title: AI trade claims casualties but the boom is far from over
full_text:
From railways to electricity and the internet, historical comparisons with the AI boom are only useful up to a point, says Nanuk Asset Management chief investment officer, Tom King.
“It’s inevitable you’ll have speculative investment failures, and it’s inevitable you’ll have periods of excess – supernormal profitability and returns that normalise, and often more than normalise, at some point,” says Mr King, who runs the $1.2bn New World Fund for the Sydney-based fund manager.
But this cycle has three crucial differences from past infrastructure booms that should make investors less fearful of a wholesale collapse, King tells The Australian.
First, there’s a common misconception that data centres could be “stranded assets”.
A data centre anywhere in the world – and potential even in space - can serve customers anywhere else, unlike a railway line or cable laid between two fixed points that may never find demand.
Second, the hardware inside those data centres – the chips doing the heavy lifting – wears out fast.
Most are being depreciated over five or six years, which means a steady replacement cycle, not a one-off splurge followed by nothing.
Third, and most importantly, despite rising bond yields, the build-out so far has not been constrained by finance. It has been constrained by a shortage of electricity.
The number of applications for grid connections in the US is about nine times the number of approvals that will get built over the next couple of years.
“If we’d had unlimited electricity supply, we’d have twice as many data centres built now as there are in existence,” Mr King says.
Because so few new facilities can be switched on, those that exist are in great demand.
Citi analysts this week said that average hourly rental prices for the latest generation Nvidia GPUs are growing at a double digits percentage pace on a week to week basis.
Where Mr King does see trouble is among highly leveraged “neocloud” operators renting out computing capacity on short-term contracts to cash-rich but unproven start-ups.
“Unless they’re still charging that in five or ten years’ time, they end up with a big valuation risk,” he says, likening the model to the US renewable energy developers that collapsed a decade ago after relying on sky-high valuations to keep raising cheap equity.
He points to Firmus Technologies – whose float was recently pulled – as the type of business most exposed, and notes credit markets are already pricing in the risk, with elevated default-insurance spreads on names including Oracle, CoreWeave and even SpaceX.
National Australia Bank is axing 2,500 jobs as it braces for a tougher economy, with 1,500 roles set to disappear before Christmas.
Crucially, Mr King doesn’t think failures there threaten the broader AI thesis.
If a neocloud operator stumbles, a hyperscaler such as Microsoft or Google is likely to simply take over the asset at a discount, because underlying demand for compute remains intact.
The trickier question, he says, is working out who pays for all this in five years’ time.
Current usage – training ever-bigger models, powering search and social media, early enterprise adoption – only accounts for part of the enormous capacity being projected for 2030.
“If you sit down with a blank sheet of paper and ask who’s going to pay for all this with revenue from AI in 2030 and beyond, it’s a bit blank,” Mr King admits.
He compares it to the launch of the iPhone, when nobody could have predicted the app economy that followed. He points to a Microsoft-backed study in the journal Science showing AI outperforming doctors on complex diagnoses as an example of value nobody is yet pricing in.
That uncertainty, Mr King says, explains the recent volatility far better than any simple bubble narrative.
So how is Nanuk playing it?
Rather than betting big on the Magnificent Seven, King’s team has aimed to stay ahead of the wave of bottlenecks as they move through the supply chain – from Nvidia’s chips, to power equipment, to memory makers such as SK Hynix, to optical networking firms, and now towards companies helping enterprises actually deploy the technology safely.
Current holdings include Japanese IT consultancy NorthSand, which is helping local businesses catch up on cloud adoption, and US back-up power supplier Generac.
Deliberately, Nanuk keeps its overall exposure to AI-linked stocks close to that of its benchmark, rather than making an all-or-nothing bet.
“We’re not necessarily going to underperform just because AI stocks underperform,” Mr King says.
The approach has paid off. The New World Fund has returned 23.5 per cent a year over three years, against 18.7 per cent for the MSCI All Country World Index, net of fees – at a time when 70 per cent of active global equity managers have trailed their benchmark.
It is a track record befitting an unusual CV.
Mr King once juggled an engineering degree with his training for the Sydney Olympic Games, where he won a gold medal for sailing.
He helped set up Nanuk in 2009 and has led its investment team for the past 12 years.
With Alphabet and Amazon plunging after their reports this week and more volatility all but guaranteed, Mr King’s message is simple: don’t bet the farm on any single AI trade, but don’t abandon the theme either. The bottlenecks will keep shifting – and so will the winners.
